books.hook: Successful investing begins with discipline, careful valuation, and protection against avoidable mistakes.

page1.inOneMinute: The Intelligent Investor presents investing as a disciplined process rather than a contest to predict market movements. Benjamin Graham distinguishes investing from speculation and stresses the importance of studying a company's value before buying its shares. His approach emphasizes a margin of safety, which means leaving room for error when estimating value. Graham also explains how emotions and changing market prices can mislead investors. The book encourages patience, diversification, and a plan that matches an investor's knowledge, resources, and tolerance for risk.
youWillGet: Recognize emotional risks in market decisions.
Build a disciplined approach to valuation.
page1.whoFor: This book suits readers who want to understand value investing and the discipline behind long-term financial decisions. It is especially useful for people willing to study financial information instead of chasing market excitement.

glance.mainIdea: Investors protect themselves through careful analysis, reasonable prices, and disciplined behavior.
glance.problem: Market excitement and fear often push people toward poorly judged financial decisions.
glance.promise: Graham offers principles for judging value and managing risk without relying on market predictions.

inside.line: Separates a reasoned investment process from attempts to profit mainly from price changes.
Distinguishes investors who prefer a simpler approach from those willing to devote more effort to analysis.
Explains why buying below a carefully estimated value creates room for mistakes.
Uses a fictional market partner to show how daily price swings can offer opportunities or distractions.
Examines emotional reactions, diversification, and the need for a plan suited to the investor.

story.heading: Define the task
story.text: Graham begins by separating investment from speculation. He argues that investing requires analysis, protection of capital, and a reasonable prospect of return. Price movement alone does not establish that a purchase is sound. Investors must understand what they own and why they bought it.

story.heading: Choose a suitable approach
story.text: The book considers different types of investors and the effort they are willing to devote. A defensive investor favors simplicity and broad protection, while an enterprising investor studies opportunities more actively. Graham's approach ties investment choices to the reader's knowledge, available time, and ability to assess risk.

story.heading: Value and a margin of safety
story.text: Graham emphasizes that market prices and underlying business value are not always the same. His margin of safety principle asks investors to leave a gap between the price paid and their estimate of value. That gap recognizes uncertainty in forecasts, financial statements, and future business conditions.

story.heading: Control your reactions
story.text: The discussion of Mr. Market illustrates the emotional pressure created by changing prices. Investors do not need to follow every swing or treat each quote as a command. Graham's broader message is to maintain a rational plan, spread risk appropriately, and resist decisions driven by excitement or panic.

author: Benjamin Graham was an influential investor, teacher, and writer associated with the development of value investing. His work focused on financial analysis, the relationship between price and business value, and methods for limiting avoidable risk. The Intelligent Investor presents these ideas for individual investors rather than only professional analysts.

Graham's approach stresses discipline over prediction. He encourages investors to examine financial facts, recognize the limits of their knowledge, and choose a strategy they can follow through changing markets. Later editions include commentary that places his principles alongside newer market conditions. Readers should separate Graham's enduring concepts from historical examples that require updating.
quickFacts: The book is a foundational work on value investing.
The margin of safety is one of Graham's central ideas.
Some editions include commentary by Jason Zweig.

lessons.title: Invest rather than speculate
lessons.text: Graham defines investing through careful analysis and a reasoned basis for expecting a return. Speculation focuses more heavily on uncertain price movements. The distinction requires investors to know the purpose of a purchase and the evidence supporting it.
lessons.example: Before buying shares, Neha reads the company's financial reports and writes down why its business interests her. She refuses to buy simply because the price has risen sharply that week.

lessons.title: Use a margin of safety
lessons.text: The margin of safety is a gap between estimated business value and the purchase price. Graham uses it to account for errors and uncertainty in analysis. It does not remove risk, but it makes the price paid central to the decision.
lessons.example: Amit estimates a business's value using its financial reports and then compares that estimate with the market price. He declines to buy when the price leaves too little room for error.

lessons.title: Understand Mr. Market
lessons.text: Graham's Mr. Market is a fictional partner whose mood changes daily. His offers sometimes reflect fear or excitement rather than a stable assessment of business value. Investors can use price changes as information without letting them dictate every decision.
lessons.example: When market prices fall on a frightening news day, Sara checks the reasons behind her original investment. She changes her decision only when the facts about the business justify it.

lessons.title: Choose your investor type
lessons.text: Graham distinguishes defensive investors from enterprising investors. The defensive approach prioritizes simplicity and reduced effort, while the enterprising approach requires deeper research. A strategy must fit the investor's time, skills, and willingness to manage decisions.
lessons.example: Vikram works long shifts and has little time to research companies. He studies diversified investment options rather than pretending he can manage a complex stock-picking routine.

lessons.title: Spread investment risk
lessons.text: Graham's principles include avoiding excessive dependence on a single holding or prediction. Diversification spreads exposure across investments, reducing the damage caused by one poor outcome. It does not guarantee gains or prevent all losses.
lessons.example: After reviewing his savings, Karan notices that nearly all his investments depend on one company. He researches diversified alternatives before making changes.

lessons.title: Manage your own behavior
lessons.text: Graham treats investor temperament as a key part of financial discipline. Fear and excitement encourage people to buy or sell at poor times. A written plan gives decisions a basis beyond the mood of the market.
lessons.example: During a sudden market rise, Asha feels tempted to abandon her plan. She rereads her investment rules and checks her goals before placing any order.

remember: A rising price does not prove sound value.
Leave room for mistakes in valuation.
Treat Mr. Market as an offer, not an authority.
Choose a strategy that fits your abilities.
Temperament matters as much as analysis.
page4.bigIdea: Disciplined investing depends on value, a margin of safety, and control over emotional decisions.
mistakes: Treating Graham's historical market examples as current investment instructions.
Assuming a margin of safety or diversification removes all investment risk.

exercises.title: Create personal investment rules

page6.whoShouldRead: Read this book if you want a foundation in value investing and disciplined financial analysis. It suits patient readers who are willing to think carefully about price, value, and risk.
page6.whoMightSkip: You may prefer a modern beginner guide if you need current, step-by-step instructions for a specific investment account. Readers seeking quick stock tips or guaranteed returns will not find that kind of promise here.

buy.suits: Buy the physical book if you want the full argument, detailed discussions, and commentary included in your chosen edition.
buy.notSuits: Skip it if you only need a brief introduction to value investing and are not ready for extended financial analysis.
buy.physicalGives: The complete text provides a fuller explanation of Graham's principles and the reasoning behind them.

books.hook: Own the market at low cost instead of trying to outsmart it.

page1.inOneMinute: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing argues that low-cost index funds offer a straightforward way to invest for the long term. John C. Bogle explains that owning a broad section of the market avoids the need to pick winning stocks or managers. Investment costs, taxes, and frequent trading reduce the share of returns investors keep. The book emphasizes patience, diversification, and the power of compounding. Its main lesson is to focus on the returns generated by businesses while keeping the costs of investing low.
youWillGet: Understand the basic idea behind index funds.
See how fees reduce investment returns.
Learn why frequent trading often hurts investors.
Explore long-term investing and asset allocation.
page1.whoFor: This book suits beginners and long-term investors who want a simple, evidence-focused approach to investing. It is especially relevant to readers who feel overwhelmed by stock tips, market predictions, and expensive financial products.

glance.mainIdea: Broad, low-cost index investing offers a practical way to capture market returns over time.
glance.problem: High fees, active trading, and attempts to beat the market reduce the returns investors keep.
glance.promise: Bogle explains how simplicity, low costs, and patience support a long-term investment plan.

story.heading: Own businesses through the market
story.text: Bogle begins with a simple argument: investors do not need to identify every future winner. A broad index fund owns a range of companies and follows a market index. This approach connects an investor's results to the combined performance of the businesses represented in that index.

story.heading: Understand where returns come from
story.text: The book separates the returns generated by businesses from changes in market prices and expectations. Bogle argues that investors should ground their expectations in business performance rather than excitement about share prices. Long-term investing requires patience when market moods change.

story.heading: Costs work against you
story.text: The discussion turns to fund expenses, taxes, trading, and manager selection. Each cost reduces the amount left for the investor. Bogle questions the idea that frequent changes or expensive funds reliably produce better results after costs.

story.heading: Keep the strategy simple
story.text: The later chapters discuss bonds, exchange-traded funds, asset allocation, and investment advice. Bogle encourages readers to build a diversified portfolio suited to their needs and maintain a long-term view. The central principle is to capture a fair share of market returns without surrendering too much to fees, taxes, and unnecessary activity.

author: John C. Bogle founded the Vanguard Group of mutual funds and served as its chairman and chief executive. He became known for promoting low-cost index investing and placing investors' interests at the center of fund design. His work challenged the assumption that professional management and frequent trading reliably improve results after costs.

The Little Book of Common Sense Investing presents Bogle's case for a broad, low-cost approach to the stock market. The revised edition expands the discussion with material on asset allocation and retirement investing. Bogle's principles focus on long-term ownership, cost control, and simplicity. Readers still need to choose investments that fit their country, financial goals, tax rules, and ability to handle losses.
quickFacts: The book's main strategy is low-cost index investing.
The revised edition includes chapters on asset allocation.

lessons.title: Own the broad market
lessons.text: Bogle favors index funds that track a broad market rather than relying on individual stock selection. This approach spreads exposure across many businesses. It does not remove market risk, but it reduces dependence on choosing a few winning companies.
lessons.example: During lunch, Riya compares a broad-market index fund with a fund holding only a few technology stocks. She considers how each choice spreads her investment risk.

lessons.title: Keep costs low
lessons.text: Fund expenses reduce the return investors keep. Bogle treats cost as one of the few parts of investing that people can directly compare and control. Small recurring charges matter because they continue to reduce the money left invested.
lessons.example: Before opening an investment account, Aman compares the annual fees and other charges of two similar funds. He records the cost differences instead of choosing the fund with the flashiest advertisement.

lessons.title: Avoid needless trading
lessons.text: Frequent trading brings transaction costs and encourages decisions based on short-term market changes. Bogle argues that investors often damage their results by trying to move in and out at the perfect time. A long-term plan reduces the urge to react to every headline.
lessons.example: When the market falls on Monday, Dev feels tempted to sell his fund. He checks his goals and planned investment period before deciding whether anything fundamental has changed.

lessons.title: Respect business returns
lessons.text: Bogle distinguishes the earnings and dividends generated by businesses from changing investor expectations. Market prices can rise or fall beyond what business results alone suggest. Long-term expectations should reflect the underlying businesses rather than assume recent price gains will continue.
lessons.example: Meera reviews a fund after a year of strong returns. She studies what drove the gains rather than assuming the same performance will repeat next year.

lessons.title: Question past winners
lessons.text: The book discusses reversion to the mean, the tendency for unusually strong or weak results to move closer to typical levels over time. Recent success alone does not prove that a fund manager will keep outperforming. Investors need a reason beyond a recent ranking to choose a fund.
lessons.example: Kunal sees a fund at the top of a performance chart. He checks its costs, investment approach, and longer record before considering it.

lessons.title: Balance stocks and bonds
lessons.text: Bogle includes asset allocation as part of a complete investing plan. Stocks and bonds behave differently, so their mix affects both risk and expected return. The appropriate balance depends on an investor's goals, time horizon, and ability to withstand losses.
lessons.example: Before investing a long-term savings pot, Farah lists when she expects to use the money and how much loss she could tolerate. She researches a stock-and-bond mix that fits those needs.

remember: Own a broad range of businesses.
Every fee reduces the return you keep.
Business results matter more than market excitement.
Past winners do not guarantee future success.
Choose an investment mix that fits your needs.
page4.bigIdea: A simple, diversified, low-cost investment strategy gives investors a practical way to pursue long-term market returns.
mistakes: Assuming an index fund prevents losses when the market falls.
Choosing a fund without checking fees, taxes, diversification, and local regulations.

page6.whoShouldRead: Read this book if you want to understand index investing, fund costs, and the logic of long-term market ownership. It suits readers who prefer a clear strategy over frequent stock picking.
page6.whoMightSkip: You may prefer a detailed technical guide if you need advanced portfolio mathematics or country-specific tax instructions. Investors seeking rapid profits or guaranteed returns will not find such a promise here.

buy.suits: Buy the physical book if you want the full argument, chapter-by-chapter explanations, and discussion of fund costs and asset allocation.
buy.notSuits: Skip it if you already understand low-cost indexing and only need a short reminder of its basic principles.
buy.physicalGives: The complete book provides the connected reasoning, market examples, and extended discussion behind Bogle's investment approach.
